The assistant to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazan-kowski) has even sent a letter to the local media explaining how they could benefit from media clips directly-not that second-hand stuff from the Parliamentary Press Gallery, in other words, the unbiased truth according to Brian.

The Tories during the election campaign promised that they would be accountable. A little more than a year later, Ministers do not answer the press, the Prime Minister avoids answering in the House, and substance has been replaced with pre-recorded clips to be sent to the regions of Canada.
Perhaps the most interesting development in the media strategy is the fact that the Prime Minister, who does not have time to be accountable to Parliament-
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, the death of Drina Joubert is being examined at an inquest which opened on
Wednesday in Toronto. Drina Joubert died on December 16 of cold and exposure in the cab of an abandoned truck in downtown Toronto. Toronto residents, who are shocked and shamed by her death and the three other deaths this year from exposure of homeless people, have formed a coalition called "Housing not Hostels". The concern is for the 6,000 to 10,000 homeless people in Toronto who cannot find accommodation now that the low rental places have been converted or destroyed. The coalition organized a march on Tuesday to City Hall to remind the public about these unnecessary deaths. It was led by several leading church people of the city of Toronto. The coalition is appearing at the current inquest, through a lawyer, in order to cross-examine witnesses, because of its conviction that it was not exposure that killed Drina Joubert but the impossibility of her getting a decent home in which to live.
Hostels are not the answer, they are the last resort. They give no privacy, no room to store belongings, they are overcrowded and there is no security while staying there. What they are demanding is that this Government and the other Governments of Canada provide housing, not hostels.
I should like to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION WESTERN PARKWAY BE RENAMED SIR JOHN A. MACDONALD PARKWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the lack of recognition in Canada of our first Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald. In most nations, a country's early leaders are honoured through national holidays or the naming of a prominent landmark in the capital city after them. In the case of Sir John we have neither. There have been several unsuccessful Bills introduced since 1979 to designate a national holiday in honour of Sir John A. Macdonald. The failure to reach agreement on these Bills may have had something to do with the fact that no one could agree on the exact date of Sir John's birthday, which is either January 10 or January 11, 1815.
As the Member of Parliament for Ottawa West I have the honour of representing essentially the same area that Sir John did toward the end of his political career. It appears to me that, if we cannot agree on a holiday, surely we could agree on designating an Ottawa landmark in his honour. We have, for example, Colonel By Drive in the city of Ottawa. In my opinion the time has come to start thinking about naming one

February 14, 1986
of Ottawa's other federally administered roadways after Sir John A. Macdonald.
I therefore call upon the National Capital Commission, at the earliest possible opportunity, to designate the scenic western portion of the Ottawa River Parkway, mostly located in my riding and Sir John A's old riding of Carleton, as the "Sir John A. Macdonald Parkway". At the same time 1 would suggest to the Commission that it consider naming the eastern portion of the Parkway after that other great Father of Confederation, Sir Georges Etienne Cartier.

subtopic: YOUNG PEOPLE'S NEED FOR BETTER ENVIRONMENT AND QUALITY OF LIFE
YOUNG PEOPLE'S NEED FOR BETTER ENVIRONMENT AND QUALITY OF LIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to draw the attention of the House to the conclusions of a study made public by the Department of National Health and Welfare on February 6 last. This study by a Queen's University social programs assessment group focuses on the troublesome problems experienced by Canadian youths. Among other findings, Mr. Speaker, nearly 50 per cent of young Canadians aged 9 to 15 do not eat properly; 25 per cent of 15-year-old teenagers smoke cigarettes and 30 per cent of them regularly drink five or more glasses of alcoholic beverages at a stretch. In addition, Mr. Speaker, 10 per cent of youngsters aged 12 smoke cigarettes, and 20 per cent of 15-year-old youths admit using cannabis.
Mr. Speaker, there is no denying that it is a social problem which concerns us all. Governments must co-operate and work together with health organizations, parents and school authorities, but it is even more imperative and urgent for each and everyone of us to do the utmost so that our troubled youths might live in a healthier environment and enjoy a better life.

subsubtopic: GRANT MADE TO GRAND CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
The question is how to throw away $30,000 of taxpayers' money? The answer is, it is very simple. You just give it to the Grand Canal Company to conduct a study on water diversions and water exports. This is the strange way the Government goes about cutting the deficit.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) cannot hide behind the excuse that this money was given by a regional office without his knowledge.
The Minister is responsible for the operations of the National Research Council. If he does not want to throw away $30,000, if he does not want to squander taxpayers' money, if he really is serious about cutting the deficit, then he has a clear choice and the power to make the necessary decision: to rescind the $30,000 grant and to ensure that the National Research Council, or any other agency under his responsibility, will not squander money on studies dealing with the export and diversions of our water resources. The message should be loud and clear. There should be no wasting of public funds to study projects that will wreak havoc on the ecology, on native lifestyles, and on Canada's long-term water interests.

Mr. Speaker, five years ago today, women from all parts of the country came to Ottawa, spontaneously and with great enthusiasm, to show their interest in improving women's legal rights as they have evolved since the suffragette movement.
By their sheer numbers, they showed politicians how determined they were to ensure the Constitution would be an effective tool for the advancement of the status of women.

We in the New Democratic Party are proud to say that we worked together with the women of Canada to ensure that Section 28 was included in the Constitution. We are continuing to speak up with the women of Canada to make the legal promise of equality an equality in fact. Unfortunately, even the progress toward formal legal equality has been painfully slow. Much remains to be done.
On the occasion of the fifth anniversary of the ad hoc conference on the Constitution, we are challenging the Government to provide stable funding to the Legal Education and Action Fund, implement the recommendations of Equality for All, establish an ongoing equality audit of laws and practices, give more importance to judicial education on equality, and appoint more women judges. subsubtopic: SIGNING OF ACCORD WITH WHITE BEAR BAND OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to announce in this House that an age-old problem with the White Bear Indian Band in Saskatchewan has been resolved.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) and Chief Brian Standingready, accompanied by 12 advisers, signed an agreement on Indian land claims representing a total value of more than $19 million.

The original grievance arises from alleged irregularities in the sale of former reserve lands of the Pheasant Rump and Ocean Man Bands when they were amalgamated with the White Bear Band in 1901.

The settlement shows the federal Government's good faith in its negotiations with official band representatives.
I want to congratulate the Minister and the band leaders on concluding this agreement.

As part of the settlement, the band will reacquire part of the former reserve lands when property known as the Lee's Ranch, comprising some 12,000 acres, is added to the reserve holdings of the White Bear Band. This land, coupled with a sizable cash compensation and other benefits, will pave the way for the White Bear Band to channel its skills and energies into achieving its goals of self-government and economic independence.

Mr. Speaker, on February 16, 1918, Lithuania became an independent kingdom, and by November of the same year Lithuania became an independent republic. For years following this historic declaration, Lithuania resisted attacks by Bolshevik troops and mercenary forces.
The years that followed were hard for this tiny nation that experienced the ravages of war and dislocation of its economy. Yet, despite this hardship, Lithuania maintained her dignity and resolve. By 1940, however, the Soviet Union overran the three Baltic States and forcibly annexed them to the Soviet Union. The popular Soviet version of these events is that the peoples of the Baltic States joined voluntarily. Historical fact is that this revision of history in Soviet textbooks is nothing more than a hoax.
Oral Questions
To Canadians of Lithuanian origin, this day commemorates the brief period of democracy enjoyed by their homeland. This day also gives reason for all Canadians to recall just how precious the gift of democracy is and how swiftly it can be lost. Let us join with Canadians of Lithuanian origin to commemorate this day and to pay tribute to their national courage and resilience. Freedom and democracy are non-negotiable commodities and they must be restored wherever they are denied.

subsubtopic: SUGAR-BEET GROWERS-CALL FOR ANNOUNCEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today Manitobans learned that the Manitoba Sugar Company, the only operational sugar refinery in western Canada, will lay off 70 of its 95 employees unless the federal Government announces a new sugar policy. Mr. Bill Siemans, President of the Canadian Sugar-beet Growers Association, has stated unequivocally that time is running out. If sugar-beet growers do not have an answer by March 1, the whole industry will be in jeopardy.
In western Canada this industry provides close to 1,600 jobs. Over the years growers have invested heavily in specialized machinery to make their industry efficient and productive.
The Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) has had over a year to find an answer to this issue. Yet his office can give the sugar-beet growers or refineries absolutely no assurance that there will be a policy decision by March 1. By this inaction, the Minister and his Government threaten the livelihood of hundreds of communities in western Canada. The western Ministers of the Government obviously do not have the clout to get a sugar policy through Cabinet.
All Members on this side of the House call upon the Government to give this issue immediate consideration and announce a decision before the Budget so that we can continue to have a thriving sugar-beet industry in western Canada.

Under the new regime, there is going to be a limit on the Questions on the Order Paper and a requirement of the quid pro quo to which I referred yesterday, a response. My own instinct is, and I think this would be the fairest for everyone concerned including members of the Opposition, that we clean the slate and let Hon. Members come forward to place their items of priority on the Order Paper. They will then be under the new regime and they can decide which ones they want and continue to replace them.
I wish to discuss another situation with the House Leaders, that is, leaving them on.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: TRANSITION TO NEW STANDING ORDERS-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext: Grandfathering them.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANSITION TO NEW STANDING ORDERS-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext:
We can certainly look at that. However, I would like to discuss the matter with the Opposition House Leaders. I think there are some down sides to that suggestion inasmuch as the costs of printing and the preoccupation with answering questions must be considered. During the experimental period we may wish to look at a way to try to resolve
Standing Orders
the priority of questions under the new regime. That is the sort of thing which I had hoped to discuss with my colleagues, the Opposition House Leaders, in order to work out some resolution.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANSITION TO NEW STANDING ORDERS-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think we should be consulting on this issue. However, since the Government House Leader placed on the record how, in a preliminary way, he was thinking of proceeding, we on our side should also place on the record, perhaps in a preliminary way as well, how we think the matter should be dealt with. We think there should be a grandfathering of the questions. That is to say all the questions on the Order Paper should remain there to be dealt with under the rules as they existed before the decision of the House yesterday, unless a Member wishes to bring forward one of these questions to be placed under the four to be handled under the new rules through the priority answering period. I think this would be the disposition of those of our members who have questions on the Order Paper. Very frankly, I will say that the Government should give serious consideration to what I have said in order to avoid the inference that perhaps the Government would not be unhappy to see those questions disappear from the Order Paper.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANSITION TO NEW STANDING ORDERS-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext: I take exception to that insinuation, Mr. Speaker. In the first place, if the Hon. Member wishes to discuss matters with me I am always available. When his Party's Whip stood up and asked me a question I tried to be as forthcoming as possible, without being devious or anything else. I simply say that it is a matter I prefer to have raised in our House Leaders' meeting. I would like to say that I am always willing to have a rational discussion about these matters. I do not want the constant insinuation that somehow there is some devious manner of thought going on on this side of the House. It is to the contrary. We are interested in accommodating Members of the House and will do what I think is fair to all Members.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANSITION TO NEW STANDING ORDERS-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, to clear the air, I wish to say that I had not intended any insinuation. I want to make that perfectly clear. I want to avoid the possibility that anyone would draw the wrong conclusion. I want it to be understood that my remarks were not for the purpose of making any insinuation. I regret that the Government House Leader interpreted them in that manner.

maintopic: TRANSITION TO NEW STANDING ORDERS-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext: On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker. In speaking on behalf of the NDP House Leader, I wish to say that we are prepared to agree with what has been suggested, especially with respect to the point that further discussions be held concerning this particular problem. I agree with the Government House Leader that this can be worked out. After all, it is an experimental period and there will be good faith expressed on both sides. It being Valentine's Day I am sure the good faith has started already. We are prepared to agree with the procedure.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary in this time of reform to which his House Leader referred a few moments ago just when the Government will answer my questions of April 2, 1985, pertaining to the costs of the Shamrock Summit. When exactly will the Government answer my question in regard to the travel of the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mrs. Blais-Grenier), the former Minister of State for Transport, when she was in the capacity of Minister of the Environment? Surely those questions can be answered. The answer to one of the questions was available to the Parliamentary Secretary at one point some four months ago. However, it was subsequently withdrawn because of a technicality. I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary if the Government will commit itself to answering these questions forthwhith.

maintopic: TRANSITION TO NEW STANDING ORDERS-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that if the Hon. Member had followed the dispute between his Party's Whip and his House Leader, he would have heard that there is now an opportunity for him, subject to negotiations going forward, and if there is unanimity in the Liberal caucus on the matter, to ask that certain questions be responded to.
It is important to put on the recond as we leave the old regime behind us that we have answered 78.4 per cent of the questions asked during this Parliament.

maintopic: TRANSITION TO NEW STANDING ORDERS-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext: What does that have to do with what I am asking? Why does the Parliamentary Secretary not say that he just does not know the answer?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: TRANSITION TO NEW STANDING ORDERS-PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS
speechtext: I rise on the same point of order, Mr. Speaker. The Parliamentary Secretary just said something which I do not think is proper. I am not in dispute with my House Leader. I asked a question in good faith. I think there is a valid question to be put as to what will happen to those questions. My House Leader tried to obtain some information from the Government House Leader in that respect. There is no dispute; it is just a matter of trying to get some facts and protection for some questions which have been on the Order Paper for a very long time. I have had one there for more than a year concerning a building which has been sold in the interim. It has not been answered.
